hints.title: Use a convenient input
hints.body: Both graphs meet at x=0, where exponential functions of this form equal 1. Compare them instead at x=1.
hints.recap: A landmark value can distinguish exponential parameters.
hints.pitfall: Agreement at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> tells you nothing about which base is larger.
hints.pause: From the drawing, is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> greater or less than a?

recall.reminder: At <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext> </mtext><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> directly reveals the base a.

hints.title: Read the base condition
hints.body: The solid graph increases, so a>1. The dashed graph is higher for positive x. If f(x)=bx, its value at 1 is b.
hints.recap: The positive-input ordering determines the order of the bases.
hints.pitfall: A base between 0 and 1 would produce a decreasing graph.
hints.pause: Which of statements 1 and 2 agrees with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>></mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>?

recall.reminder: For bases above 1, exponentiation preserves exponent order.

hints.title: Translate the input multiplier
hints.body: At x=1, the alternative form has value ak. Compare this with a using the monotonicity implied by the solid graph.
hints.recap: An input multiplier changes the effective exponential base.
hints.pitfall: Check the base range before converting a power comparison to an exponent comparison.
hints.pause: Derive the permitted multiplier range and combine it with your base comparison.

recall.reminder: An input multiplier changes the effective exponential base.

solution:
The solid exponential is increasing, so a>1. At x=1 the diagram gives f(1)>a.

If f(x)=bx, then f(1)=b, so b>a: statement 1 is possible and 2 is not.

If f(x)=akx, then f(1)=ak. Because a>1, ak>a holds exactly when k>1: statement 3 is possible and 4 is not. In fact akx=(ak)x, so these two descriptions agree.

1 and 3 only: E.
knowledgePattern: Compare bases and input scale from two crossing exponential graphs
